questions.stem: Metformin lowers hepatic fatty acid synthesis mainly because AMPK activation causes which change?

options.A: Phosphorylation and inactivation of acetyl-CoA carboxylase
options.B: Allosteric activation of ACC by citrate
options.D: Increased fatty acid synthase expression through SREBP-1

questions.explanation: Metformin raises AMP/ATP, activating AMPK, which phosphorylates and inactivates ACC, so less malonyl-CoA (and less fat) is made. B: Citrate activates ACC, the opposite of AMPK's effect. C: HMG-CoA synthase belongs to ketogenesis. D: SREBP-1 is driven by insulin and would raise synthesis. E: HSL mobilizes stored TAG and isn't the mechanism here.

questions.stem: An 18-month-old vomits and sleeps through breakfast, then is found unresponsive with glucose 1.8 mmol/L. Free fatty acids are high, ketones are low, and the acylcarnitine profile shows medium-chain species. His sister died suddenly in infancy. Which enzyme is deficient?
questions.explanation: High FFAs show mobilization works; low ketones and medium-chain acylcarnitines show β-oxidation stalling at medium chain length: MCAD deficiency. A: CPT-I deficiency gives low acylcarnitines (they are never made). C: This ketogenesis step wouldn't produce medium-chain acylcarnitines. D: CPT-II deficiency raises C16/C18 acylcarnitines and mainly hits muscle. E: Glycogen phosphorylase deficiency causes fasting hypoglycemia with intact fat oxidation and raised ketones.

questions.stem: Which molecule is both the committed product of fatty acid synthesis and the inhibitor of the carnitine shuttle?
questions.explanation: Malonyl-CoA is made by ACC and inhibits CPT-I, so newly made palmitate cannot be burned. A: Citrate activates ACC and carries acetyl units to the cytosol. B: Acetyl-CoA is the substrate of ACC, not a CPT-I inhibitor. D: Acylcarnitine is the product of CPT-I. E: Long-chain acyl-CoA inhibits ACC and is the CPT-I substrate.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old woman develops thigh pain and dark urine after a 9-hour hike with little food. CK is 48,000 U/L. She had similar episodes with fasting and fever, never with short intense exercise, and is normal between attacks. Long-chain (C16, C18) acylcarnitines are raised. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Prolonged effort or fasting forces muscle onto long-chain fatty acids, and a CPT-II defect raises long-chain acylcarnitines: CPT-II deficiency. A: McArdle is triggered by brief maximal effort, has a second wind, and CK stays raised between attacks. C: CPT-I deficiency affects the liver and gives low acylcarnitines. D: MCAD gives medium-chain species and presents with infant fasting hypoglycemia. E: Von Gierke gives fasting hypoglycemia with lactic acidosis and hepatomegaly, not recurrent rhabdomyolysis.

questions.stem: A patient with vitamin B12 deficiency excretes methylmalonate. Which step of odd-chain fatty acid oxidation is blocked?
questions.explanation: Methylmalonyl-CoA mutase needs the B12 coenzyme; when it fails, methylmalonate and propionate are excreted. A: Propionyl-CoA carboxylase needs biotin. B: The racemase needs no vitamin cofactor. C: This is the ACC step of fatty acid synthesis (biotin). E: This is ketogenesis, unrelated to B12.

questions.stem: Why can the liver produce ketone bodies but not use them as fuel?
questions.explanation: Liver mitochondria have no thiophorase (succinyl-CoA:acetoacetate CoA transferase), the enzyme that activates acetoacetate to acetoacetyl-CoA in peripheral tissues. B: HMG-CoA synthase is the liver's rate-limiting ketogenic enzyme. C: Hepatocytes have mitochondria (red blood cells don't). D: This enzyme interconverts acetoacetate and 3-hydroxybutyrate, depending on NAD⁺/NADH. E: Ketone bodies are released into blood and used by brain, muscle and kidney.

questions.stem: A patient on fat-free parenteral nutrition for 8 months develops scaly dermatitis. Which fatty acid appears in their blood?
questions.explanation: Without linoleate, desaturases act on oleate instead, producing Mead acid, which is diagnostic of essential fatty acid deficiency. A: Arachidonic acid is made from linoleate, so it falls. B: Phytanic acid accumulates in Refsum disease. C: α-Linolenic acid is an essential fatty acid and would also be absent. D: Very-long-chain fatty acids accumulate in peroxisomal disorders such as Zellweger and X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy.

questions.stem: Adipocytes can store fatty acids as triacylglycerol only when glucose enters them. Why can't they use free glycerol instead?

options.E: Hormone-sensitive lipase is active after meals

questions.explanation: Adipocytes have no glycerol kinase, so glycerol phosphate must come from glucose via DHAP, and glucose enters through insulin-dependent GLUT4; the liver has glycerol kinase. A: They need this enzyme to reduce DHAP, so they have it. B: Fatty acids must be activated to acyl-CoA in all tissues that make TAG. C: Adipocytes do have GLUT4; it is how glucose enters. E: HSL is dephosphorylated and inactive when insulin is high.

questions.stem: A patient with the muscle form of CPT-II deficiency is advised to take medium-chain triglyceride supplements. Why do they help?

options.B: Medium-chain fatty acids inhibit malonyl-CoA formation
options.D: They are converted to muscle glycogen
options.E: They stimulate carnitine synthesis in muscle

questions.explanation: Fatty acids shorter than 12 carbons cross the inner mitochondrial membrane and are activated in the matrix, bypassing CPT-I, the translocase and CPT-II. A: They bypass the defective enzyme; they don't repair it. B: Their oxidation doesn't depend on CPT-I, so malonyl-CoA is irrelevant to them. D: Fatty acids can't make net glucose or glycogen. E: Muscle can't synthesize carnitine; liver and kidney make it.
